name: Apache Polaris
license: Apache 2.0 (since the first public release in July 2024)
summary: An open-source Iceberg REST catalog: one server that every engine asks where a table’s current metadata is, with role-based access control and short-lived storage credentials per table.
intro: Polaris is a Java 21 server (built on Quarkus) that implements the Apache Iceberg REST catalog protocol on port 8181, plus its own management API. An engine such as Spark, Flink, Trino, Snowflake or PyIceberg asks it to create, load or commit a table; Polaris keeps the pointer to each table’s current metadata file and swaps it atomically on commit. The data and Iceberg metadata stay in your S3, Azure or Google Cloud Storage bucket. Polaris’s own state (catalogs, nested namespaces, tables, views, principals, roles, grants and policies) lives in a metastore: PostgreSQL through JDBC for production, MongoDB as an experimental option, or memory, the default, which loses everything on restart. Access works in layers: privileges such as `TABLE_READ_DATA` are granted to catalog roles, catalog roles to principal roles, and principal roles to principals (users or services that log in with OAuth client credentials). When a principal loads a table, Polaris can vend credentials: it calls AWS STS `AssumeRole` with a session policy scoped to that table’s location, or issues an Azure user delegation SAS or a downscoped Google token, so the engine never holds broad bucket keys. One server can host several isolated tenants, called realms, each with its own catalogs.

A catalog can also be external, mirroring tables another catalog owns as read-only, and federation can forward requests to another Iceberg REST catalog such as AWS Glue, or to Hive Metastore or BigQuery Metastore in a custom build. Generic tables register Delta Lake or CSV tables by location (in beta), and policies record compaction, snapshot expiry and orphan-file rules, but Polaris doesn’t run them: Spark, Trino or a tool such as Floe has to read and apply them. Snowflake built Polaris, open-sourced it in July 2024 and donated it to the Apache Software Foundation, where it graduated to a top-level project in February 2026. It is free to run yourself. Snowflake sells it as Snowflake Open Catalog, which no longer accepts new customers, and has built it into Snowflake Horizon Catalog; Dremio’s built-in catalog is also based on it.
strengths: Implements the Iceberg REST protocol, so one catalog serves Spark, Flink, Trino, Snowflake, Dremio, PyIceberg and any other REST client
Access control in one place for every engine, enforced by handing out short-lived storage credentials scoped to the tables a principal may read or write
Vendor-neutral governance: an Apache top-level project since February 2026, with developers from Snowflake, Dremio and others, under Apache 2.0
Several catalogs and isolated realms on one server, federation with Glue, Hive Metastore and BigQuery Metastore, and Open Policy Agent for external authorization
limits: It doesn’t maintain tables: compaction, snapshot expiry and orphan-file cleanup still need Spark, Trino or another tool, even when a policy describes them
Defaults are for development: the in-memory metastore loses data on restart and random signing keys break multi-replica setups; production needs PostgreSQL, fixed keys and realm settings
Its permissions hold only if each table’s files sit in their own directory that mirrors the namespace tree, and only for engines that use the credentials it vends rather than their own bucket keys
Support beyond Iceberg is thin: generic tables for Delta Lake and CSV are in beta, the MongoDB metastore is experimental, and Hive and BigQuery federation need a custom build
Snowflake Open Catalog, the hosted version, is closed to new customers; Snowflake now points them to Horizon Catalog

snippet.title: Create a catalog, give a read-only role to an analyst, and query it from Spark
source: pip install apache-polaris                 # the Polaris CLI
export CLIENT_ID=root CLIENT_SECRET=s3cr3t  # admin credentials for the server on localhost:8181
# privilege -> catalog role -> principal role -> principal
polaris principals create analyst        # prints the analyst's clientId and clientSecret
polaris catalog-roles grant --catalog lake --principal-role analysts sales_reader
polaris privileges namespace grant --namespace sales --catalog lake \
# the analyst connects with their own credentials; Polaris vends short-lived S3 keys

sections.title: Other Iceberg REST catalogs
sections.intro: Any of these can sit where Polaris sits: engines speak the same REST protocol to all of them.

items.name: AWS Glue Iceberg REST endpoint
items.text: The Glue Data Catalog answers the Iceberg REST protocol at `https://glue.<region>.amazonaws.com/iceberg`, for Iceberg tables in S3 and S3 Tables. Nothing to run, but the endpoint is regional and serves one AWS account’s Data Catalog.

items.name: Lakekeeper
items.text: An Iceberg REST catalog written in Rust, with access control and credential vending; a commercial Lakekeeper+ edition comes from Vakamo.

items.name: Unity Catalog OSS
items.text: The open-source Unity Catalog, a sandbox project at the LF AI & Data Foundation. It registers Delta Lake tables, and Iceberg and Hudi through UniForm, answers the Iceberg REST and Hive metastore APIs, and also catalogs files, functions and AI models.

items.name: Project Nessie
items.text: A catalog with Git-like branches and multi-table commits, created by Dremio’s founders. Dremio said in 2024 it would bring Nessie’s features into Polaris.

story: By 2024 Iceberg had become the table format most engines could read and write, but each engine still had to agree on a catalog, the service that says which metadata file is a table’s current version. The Iceberg community had written an open REST protocol for catalogs, yet most implementations were tied to one vendor or covered only part of the protocol. Snowflake argued that these limits recreated the lock-in open table formats were meant to remove.

At its June 2024 Summit, Snowflake announced Polaris Catalog: a full implementation of the Iceberg REST protocol with its own role-based security, designed to run on Snowflake’s infrastructure or your own. It published the code under Apache 2.0 on 30 July 2024, opened a hosted preview the same day, and Dremio said it would fold the ideas of its Nessie catalog into the project. In August 2024 Polaris entered the Apache Incubator, with a core team drawn mostly from Snowflake and Dremio; the proposal admitted that diversifying beyond those two companies was its main risk.

The first Apache release, 0.9.0-incubating, came in February 2025 and 1.0 in July 2025. Polaris graduated to a top-level Apache project in February 2026, and by then both Snowflake’s and Dremio’s own catalogs were built on it.

choices.choice: The whole Iceberg REST protocol, not a subset
choices.why: The proposal set out to be a full, production-ready reference implementation: if something is in the spec, it should work in Polaris, so any REST-compatible engine can use it without vendor-specific gaps.
The REST protocol said little about authorization. Polaris added a role-based model and credential vending so access rules are enforced the same way whichever engine reads the table.
Snowflake wanted to host it as a service, so one deployment serves many catalogs and users, with realms keeping tenants apart in the same database.
A catalog meant to be vendor-neutral needed governance no single company controls. Snowflake granted the code and donated its “POLARIS CATALOG” trademark application to the foundation.
